clue.text: Stop meeting of tart and fraudster

parts.note: PRO is short for prostitute, a slang sense of tart
a rogue is a dishonest swindler

explanation.surface: Someone calls off a gathering involving a loose woman and a con man.
explanation.walkthrough: To prorogue a parliament is to end its session without dissolving it.
explanation.definitionFit: Proroguing a legislature discontinues its sitting, so it is a formal way to halt a meeting.

clue.text: Surprise as foot's first amputated at hospital

indicators.note: the opening letter is cut off like a limb, so the word for foot loses its initial

parts.note: an iambus is a metrical foot in verse, one short syllable then one long

explanation.surface: An unexpected amputation of the front of the foot happens at a hospital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Foot' is the poetic foot IAMBUS, not a limb; 'first amputated' cuts its I, leaving AMBUS.
explanation.definitionFit: An ambush is a surprise attack, so the noun works as a synonym of surprise.

clue.text: Horse lands escapee unfortunately in battle

indicators.note: things going badly suggests the letters end up in a jumbled order

parts.note: horse is slang for heroin, abbreviated H

explanation.surface: A horse unluckily brings an escaped prisoner ashore during a battle.
explanation.walkthrough: H, LANDS and ESCAPEE are rearranged together by 'unfortunately'.
explanation.definitionFit: Passchendaele was a First World War battle near Ypres in 1917, so the name is an example of a battle.

clue.text: Turn on soldier and look for escort

indicators.note: in an across clue one piece placed on another follows it

parts.note: GI is an American soldier
a turn in a game is a go
lo is an old word meaning look or behold

explanation.surface: Someone rounds on a soldier and seeks a companion for the evening.
explanation.definitionFit: A gigolo is a man paid to act as a woman's companion, a hired escort.

clue.text: Correct number working over lunchtime maybe

parts.note: a machine that is on is working

indicators.note: over signals that the word for correct is turned back to front

parts.note: to edit is to correct text

explanation.surface: Someone fixes a figure while working through the lunch break.
explanation.definitionFit: Noontide is midday, the time when lunch is usually taken, hence the 'maybe'.

clue.text: Flier looking angry with naval officer

parts.note: someone red in the face looks angry
an admiral is a senior naval officer

explanation.surface: An airman glares crossly alongside a senior officer of the navy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flier' suggests an aviator, but it is a butterfly.
explanation.definitionFit: The red admiral is a common butterfly, and butterflies fly, so it is a flier.

clue.text: Cautious, being out of position when first pair swapped

indicators.note: exchanging the opening two letters moves the first one back a place

parts.note: wary means cautious

explanation.surface: A careful person feels misplaced once the leading couple trade places.
explanation.walkthrough: Swapping the W and A at the start of WARY gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Something askew or amiss is out of its proper position, which is the adjective's sense.

clue.text: Charge laid down by one carrier …

indicators.note: the word for charge is set down by the word for one, so it comes first in the answer

parts.note: a tax is a charge levied by the state
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A fee is imposed by one transport company.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links this clue's surface to the next one but plays no part in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A cab carries passengers for hire, so it is a carrier.

clue.text: … dealing with supply in the neighbourhood, the main point I included

indicators.note: the outer word for nearby has the inner pieces included within it

parts.note: local means in the neighbourhood
the gist is the main point of something

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue, a supply operation nearby includes the key point and me.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis joins this surface to the previous clue; 'included' signals the container.
explanation.definitionFit: Logistics is the organisation of supplies, so the adjective means concerned with supply.

clue.text: With science, one may be doing this to someone very bright

definitions.text: With science, one may be doing this to someone very bright

parts.words: With science, one may be doing this to someone very bright
parts.note: a phrase meaning to baffle with jargon pairs with the dazzling effect a brilliant light has on the eyes

explanation.walkthrough: 'Blinding with science' means bewildering someone with technical talk; a very bright light also does this to the eyes, and the clue's 'someone very bright' is a clever person.
explanation.definitionFit: Dazzling with jargon and dazzling with light both describe depriving someone of sight or understanding.

clue.text: One pickled in the pub? He may have no choice!

indicators.note: the pickled item sits inside the word for the pub

parts.note: a bar is a pub or drinking place
a pickled egg is a traditional pub snack

explanation.surface: A drunk in the pub might have no option left.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pickled' looks like drunk, but it refers to a pickled egg. The definition plays on the saying 'beggars can't be choosers'.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb says beggars cannot be choosers, so a mendicant is someone with no choice.

clue.text: No actual recollection where information is stored?

parts.note: virtual means not actual, existing only in effect
a memory is a recollection

explanation.surface: Not really remembering where the data was put.
explanation.definitionFit: In computing, virtual memory is disk space used as an extension of main storage, a place data is held.

clue.text: In farmland, a mob, only one British

indicators.note: of the two Bs in the word for mob, only one B for British is kept

parts.note: a rabble is a disorderly mob

explanation.surface: Out in the fields, a crowd gathers that has just one Briton among them.
explanation.walkthrough: RABBLE has two Bs (B = British); keeping 'only one' gives RABLE.
explanation.definitionFit: Arable land is ground ploughed for crops, and the word stands as a noun for such land.

clue.text: Safely stored warmth in building

indicators.note: the word for warmth sits inside the word for building

parts.note: a shed is a simple building
heat is warmth

explanation.surface: Something is kept secure with heating in an outbuilding.
explanation.definitionFit: A sword in its scabbard is sheathed, put away safely in a protective cover.

clue.text: Salesman gets more money for extra performance

parts.note: REP is short for a sales representative
a rise is a pay increase

explanation.surface: A sales rep earns a pay increase for doing an encore.
explanation.definitionFit: A reprise is a repeated performance of a piece, an extra rendition.

clue.text: Give speechifying a break, as happened to the Stuarts

parts.note: a rest is a break
oration is formal speechmaking

explanation.surface: Advice to pause the speeches, citing the experience of a royal dynasty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Give' is a link. The Stuart monarchy was restored in 1660 when Charles II returned.
explanation.definitionFit: The Stuarts were returned to the throne in 1660, an event known historically by this name.

clue.text: Good start to climb, say — going up, I can walk across ceiling?

indicators.note: in a down clue going up means the letters read from bottom to top

parts.note: OK means good or acceptable

indicators.note: the opening letter of the next word is taken

parts.note: EG, for example, is what say means

explanation.surface: A climber boasts of a fine start, hoping to cross a ceiling while ascending.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going up' turns OK, C and EG backwards in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Geckos have sticky toe pads that let these small lizards scamper upside down across ceilings.

clue.text: Queen is first to encourage and tend soldiers

indicators.note: the first letter of the following word is taken

parts.note: to lean towards something is to tend towards it
OR stands for other ranks, ordinary soldiers

explanation.surface: A queen is the first to inspire and care for the troops.
explanation.definitionFit: Eleanor of Aquitaine and Eleanor of Castile were English queens, so the name exemplifies a queen.

clue.text: Lion-tamer also about to break into parts in drama

parts.note: and means also

indicators.note: the short word for about breaks into the word for theatrical parts

parts.note: roles are parts played in a drama
C stands for circa, Latin for about

explanation.surface: A lion-tamer is about to burst into a dramatic part as well.
explanation.walkthrough: Androcles, in the old fable, befriended a lion by pulling a thorn from its paw.
explanation.definitionFit: The fabled slave tamed a lion by kindness, so a lion-tamer describes him loosely.

clue.text: I'm off for a run

definitions.meaning: said when leaving, a farewell like goodbye
in cricket a run scored from a ball that passes the batsman untouched

explanation.walkthrough: Cricket: a bye is a run scored without the batsman hitting the ball.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a parting word and a cricket extra counted as a run.

clue.text: An extravagant poet?

definitions.meaning: an extravagant person, one who lavishes money
Stephen ... was an English poet of the 1930s generation

explanation.definitionFit: A wasteful person splashes cash, and the surname is that of the poet Stephen Spender.

clue.text: In remote place of business, ring to get gin brought round? No way!

indicators.note: the word for gin is brought around the word for ring, enclosing it

parts.note: a gin is a snare or trap for game
a ding is the ring of a bell
O, nought, means no or nothing
ST is short for street, a way

explanation.surface: Out in the wilds, can you phone for gin delivery? Not a chance!
explanation.walkthrough: 'gin' is not the drink but a snare, and 'brought round' makes it enclose the ring; 'In' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A trading post was a store set up in remote frontier country for bartering goods.

clue.text: Great number last month overcome by unusual tedium

indicators.note: the abbreviation is overcome, surrounded, by the rearranged letters
an unusual version suggests the letters are rearranged

parts.note: ULT, ultimo, means last month in old business letters

explanation.surface: A crowd last month succumbs to strange boredom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unusual' rearranges the boredom word to MITUDE, and 'overcome by' sets the old business abbreviation inside it after the M.
explanation.definitionFit: A multitude is a great many, a crowd or a vast number.

clue.text: After expelling outsiders, poll very shortly concluded

indicators.note: the first and last letters of the word for poll are thrown out

parts.note: a ballot is a poll or vote

indicators.note: cut short, the word loses its final letter

parts.note: taken as written before trimming

explanation.surface: Once the extremists are expelled, the vote is very soon finished.
explanation.walkthrough: BALLOT less B and T gives ALLO; VERY less Y gives VER.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying it's all over means a thing is finished or concluded.

clue.text: Looks amazed at what swimmer may be wearing

explanation.definitionFit: To goggle is to stare wide-eyed, and goggles are protective glasses worn by swimmers.

clue.text: Deconstruct articles intelligently at last in college

parts.note: AN and A are both indefinite articles

indicators.note: the picked letter is placed inside the abbreviation for the college

parts.note: LSE is the London School of Economics

indicators.note: the final letter of the word is taken

explanation.surface: Break down articles cleverly, eventually, at a college.
explanation.walkthrough: LSE, the London School of Economics, is a college of London University.
explanation.definitionFit: To analyse something is to break it into parts to understand it, close to deconstruct.

clue.text: Cockney's to take in the air noisily — it makes a long sound

indicators.note: a Cockney accent turns the TH sound into a V sound
noisily signals that the word is spoken aloud

parts.note: to breathe is to take in air

explanation.surface: A Londoner gasps for air loudly, making a long note.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockney: the working-class East London accent, where 'th' is said as 'v'.
explanation.definitionFit: A breve is a musical note worth two semibreves, the longest in common use.

clue.text: Advice to Aladdin creates difficulty

definitions.meaning: Aladdin summoned the genie by rubbing his magic lamp
as in 'there's the ...', an obstacle or snag

explanation.definitionFit: Aladdin is told to stroke the lamp, and in Hamlet the word means an obstacle.
